# ChemiCompiler
The ChemiCompiler is a chemistry machine you program instead of click. It holds ten beakers, and runs short programs that move reagents between them, heat them, and package the results into pills, vials or medical patches.
Build one from a [bold]ChemiCompiler M7 machine board[/bold], printed at a medical lathe.
# The Interface
The big box at the top is where you write code. It is not saved anywhere until you put it in a slot.
Below it are [bold]Save[/bold], [bold]Load[/bold], and six numbered slots. The slot buttons do whatever the Save and Load buttons say they do:
- With neither pressed, clicking a slot [bold]runs[/bold] the program in it. - With Save pressed, clicking a slot stores the code from the editor into it. - With Load pressed, clicking a slot pulls its code back into the editor.
Slots holding a program are highlighted green. The Halt button stops a running program early.
Below those are the ten reservoirs, r1 to r10. Click one with a beaker in hand to load it, click it empty-handed to take the beaker back. Full reservoirs are highlighted blue. Under them are the registers, which only update when a program stops. That makes them a debugger of last resort: run a program, see where the registers ended up, work out where it went wrong.
The right-hand corner lists the materials loaded into the machine.
While a program is running everything is locked, including the beakers.
# Memory
A program has 1024 memory cells, each holding a number from 0 to 255, and a pointer that starts at the first one. Almost every instruction works on whichever cell the pointer is currently sitting on.
There is no way to type a number directly. If you want a cell to hold 25, you write twenty-five [bold]+[/bold] signs. This is not a mistake, it is the whole personality of the language. Copy and paste is your friend.
# Registers
Three registers decide what the chemistry instructions actually do:
- [bold]sx[/bold], the source. Which reservoir, 1 to 10, an instruction reads from. - [bold]tx[/bold], the target. Where things go. 1 to 10 for a reservoir, 11 for the pill generator, 12 for the vial generator, 13 to throw it away, and 14 to 17 for the patch generators: 14 a patch, 15 a rapid patch, 16 a large patch, 17 a therapeutic patch. - [bold]ax[/bold], the amount. How many units to move, and how far to heat.
You set them by putting a number in a memory cell and then copying that cell into the register.
# Materials
The pill generator is free, but everything else the machine prints costs the same materials it would cost to print at a lathe. Load sheets into the machine by hand; what it is holding shows in the corner of the interface.
- A vial costs 1 glass. - Any patch costs 1 cloth and 1 plastic.
Each of those makes one container per instruction,with however much you sent it. Anything that will not fit goes back to the reservoir it came from. If the materials aren't there the instruction fails like any other: the machine buzzes, your reagents stay where they were, and the program carries on regardless.
# Instructions
Anything that isn't an instruction is ignored, so you can leave spaces and notes in your programs.
## Pointer and arithmetic
- [bold]\>[/bold] move the pointer one cell right - [bold]\<[/bold] move the pointer one cell left - [bold]+[/bold] add one to the current cell - [bold]-[/bold] subtract one from the current cell
## Loops
- [bold]\[[/bold] if the current cell is zero, skip past the matching \] - [bold]\][/bold] if the current cell is not zero, jump back to the matching \[
Loops nest. A program with brackets that don't pair up is refused rather than run, so a stray \] will not brick the machine. A program that loops forever is abandoned after ten minutes.
## Registers
Each register has one instruction to write it from the current cell, and one to read it back into the cell.
- [bold]}[/bold] and [bold]{[/bold] write and read [bold]sx[/bold] - [bold])[/bold] and [bold]([/bold] write and read [bold]tx[/bold] - [bold]'[/bold] and [bold]^[/bold] write and read [bold]ax[/bold]
The brace-style symbol of each pair writes the register from memory; the other reads it back. A program that appears to run cleanly but moves nothing has almost always got one of these pairs the wrong way round.
## Chemistry
- [bold],[/bold] measure how full reservoir sx is and put that number in ax - [bold]$[/bold] bring reservoir sx to (273 - tx) + ax Kelvin. Takes a few seconds. To heat rather than cool, leave tx at 0 and put the temperature above freezing in ax. - [bold]@[/bold] move ax units from reservoir sx to wherever tx points - [bold]#[/bold] move ax units of one single reagent from sx to tx. Which reagent is taken from the current memory cell, counting from 1, in the order they are listed in the beaker.
Anything that will not fit in the target goes back where it came from. Reagents are never quietly lost, except at the ejection port, which is what the ejection port is for.
## Everything else
- [bold].[/bold] add the current cell to a line of text, as a character. Writing a newline (10) makes the machine say the line out loud; anything still unsaid is spoken when the program stops. - [bold]~[/bold] lock this program so Load can no longer read it back. It can still be overwritten. - [bold]*[/bold] pauses briefly, for reactions that take time.
# Speed
Instructions are not free. Moving the pointer and counting up and down are quick, shuffling registers costs a little more, and anything that reaches into a beaker — transferring, isolating, measuring — takes about half a second on its own. Standing still on purpose with [bold]*[/bold] is the slowest single instruction there is, at a full second.
That means the expensive part of a program is the chemistry, not the arithmetic, which is how it should be. Don't agonise over shaving \+ signs off your constants; think about how many times you're moving reagents.
Heating is slower still. The machine pushes heat at the same rate a hotplate does, so bringing a full beaker up to reaction temperature takes the better part of a minute. Automating chemistry saves you clicking, not time.
# Sounds
You cannot see the registers while a program runs, so listening to the machine is how you follow it.
- Two beeps as a program starts. - One beep every time reagents leave a reservoir, whether they go to another beaker, a pill, a vial, a patch or the bin. Count them against your plan and you know how far it has got. - A low beep when heating begins, and the same low beep again once the reservoir is up to temperature. Silence between the two is normal; heating is slow. - A high beep when the program finishes and the beakers unlock. - A buzzer when an instruction could not be carried out. This is the one to listen for.
# Failures
If an instruction can't be carried out, usually because sx or tx points at a reservoir with no beaker in it, or because the machine has run out of the materials a vial or patch needs, it beeps loudly and carries straight on to the next instruction. It does not stop. A program that buzzes repeatedly is a program that is doing nothing at all, very confidently.
# Writing a program
Plan on paper first. Seriously. Write down every beaker, what is in it, how full it is, and every transfer in order, before you write a single symbol. Then translate the plan one line at a time.
A useful opening move is to fill the first several cells with small numbers you'll need later:
[bold]+\>++\>+++\>++++\>+++++[/bold]
That leaves 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 in the first five cells, which are exactly the reservoir numbers you will be loading into sx and tx all program. Add whatever transfer amounts you need on the end, and from then on setting a register is just walking the pointer to the right cell and copying it.
